[Containerlab](https://containerlab.dev) builds network labs out of containers. You describe the routers, switches
and hosts and the links between them in one YAML file. Containerlab starts the nodes, wires them together and gives
each one a management address. One command brings the lab up, and one takes it down.

This is the first part of the Containerlab workshop. All the instructions are for **Ubuntu Linux** (22.04, 24.04 or
26.04 LTS, desktop or server). By the end of it you will have:

- Docker and Containerlab installed on an Ubuntu host
- your user able to run labs without typing `sudo`
- a two-node lab deployed, tested and removed

## What you need

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Host | An Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04 or 26.04 LTS machine or VM. Use x86_64: many network OS images, Cisco XRd among them, are not built for ARM64 |
| Access | A user with `sudo` rights |
| CPU | More than 1 vCPU. Most network OS containers need at least one core each while booting |
| Memory | Depends on the lab. A Linux node needs a few MB; a Cisco XRd router about **1.6 GB** in the labs of this workshop, and up to 2.5 GB when it runs routing protocols |
| Router image | Parts 2 to 5 use Cisco XRd, which you get from Cisco with your own account ([Part 2](../02-load-images/) shows how). Part 1 needs no vendor image |
| IPv6 | Must not be disabled in the kernel |
| Internet | To download packages and container images |

For this workshop, a host with **4 vCPUs and 16 GB of RAM** is enough for every lab.

::: {.callout-note}
## How big a lab can one host run?
On a mini PC with a Ryzen 7 255 and 64 GB of RAM, a 15-router Cisco XRd lab uses about 34 GB of memory and runs
comfortably. Memory, not CPU, is usually what limits how many nodes fit on one host.
:::

## Before you start

Install `curl` and `git`, which the steps below use. Ubuntu Server usually has them; Ubuntu Desktop may not:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y curl git
```

Then choose **one** of the two options below.

## Option A: the quick setup script

On a fresh Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04 host, one command installs everything: Docker CE, Docker Compose, Containerlab and
the GitHub `gh` CLI.

```bash
curl -sL https://containerlab.dev/setup | sudo -E bash -s "all"
```

The script also raises the SSH server's maximum login attempts, which helps when you SSH into many lab nodes. To skip
that change, run `export SETUP_SSHD="false"` first.

Then log out and back in, so that your user's new groups (`docker` and `clab_admins`) take effect, and go to
[Check the installation](#check-the-installation). If `id -nG` still does not list both groups, reboot.

The script is tested on Ubuntu up to 24.04. On Ubuntu 26.04, use Option B.

## Option B: step by step

These steps work on every supported Ubuntu release, and are the ones used on the workshop host (Ubuntu 26.04). Each
step shows what is being installed, so use this route if you want to know exactly what changed on your system.

### 1. Install Docker

Ubuntu's own `docker.io` package is enough for Containerlab:

```bash
sudo apt install -y docker.io
sudo usermod -aG docker "$USER"
```

The last command lets your user run `docker` without `sudo`. If you prefer Docker's own packages (`docker-ce`),
follow [Docker's install guide](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/) instead; either works.

### 2. Add the Containerlab package repository and install

Containerlab is published in its own APT repository:

```bash
echo "deb [trusted=yes] https://netdevops.fury.site/apt/ /" | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/netdevops.list

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y containerlab
```

Installing from the repository means later upgrades arrive with your normal `apt upgrade`.

### 3. Log out and back in

The installer adds your user to a group called `clab_admins`, and step 1 added you to `docker`. New group
memberships only apply to new login sessions, so log out and log back in.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Still missing the groups after logging back in?
On a desktop session, background user services can survive a logout and keep the old group list. If
`id -nG` still does not show `docker` and `clab_admins` after logging back in, reboot the host.
:::

## Check the installation

```bash
containerlab version
id -nG
docker ps
```

You should see:

- a version banner from `containerlab version` (0.82 or newer at the time of writing)
- `docker` and `clab_admins` in the output of `id -nG`
- an empty table from `docker ps`, not a "permission denied" error

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why no sudo?
Containerlab is installed as a root-owned SUID binary. Members of `clab_admins` can run commands that change the
host, such as `deploy` and `destroy`. Everyone else can only run read-only commands such as `inspect`. Membership is
effectively root access to the host, so add only people you trust.
:::

## Run a first lab

The workshop repository has a two-node lab to prove that everything works: two small Alpine Linux containers joined by
one link.

```yaml
name: first-lab

topology:
  nodes:
    n1:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3
      exec:
        - ip addr add 10.0.12.1/30 dev eth1
    n2:
      kind: linux
      image: alpine:3
      exec:
        - ip addr add 10.0.12.2/30 dev eth1

  links:
    - endpoints: ["n1:eth1", "n2:eth1"]
```

To see this lab drawn as a diagram, open it in the [topology viewer](https://graphs.dynanet.dev/topology?example=first). You can paste any
topology file there; it is read in your browser and nothing is uploaded.

### Deploy

Get the workshop files into your home folder, then deploy the lab. Every later part uses this same copy, in
`~/dynanet-dev`:

```bash
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/aghufran/dynanet-dev.git
cd ~/dynanet-dev/clab-workshop/labs/01-first-lab
containerlab deploy -t first-lab.clab.yml
```

Containerlab pulls the Alpine image, starts both nodes, creates the link and prints a table of the nodes with their
management addresses. Each node is a container named `clab-<lab name>-<node name>`.

### Verify

Run each check from the host. Each node is a container, so `docker exec` runs a command inside it.

| Step | Command | You should see |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Nodes running | `containerlab inspect --all` | `clab-first-lab-n1` and `clab-first-lab-n2`, both `running` |
| 2. Address on n1 | `docker exec clab-first-lab-n1 ip -4 addr show eth1` | `inet 10.0.12.1/30` |
| 3. Address on n2 | `docker exec clab-first-lab-n2 ip -4 addr show eth1` | `inet 10.0.12.2/30` |
| 4. Reachability | `docker exec clab-first-lab-n1 ping -c 3 10.0.12.2` | `3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0% packet loss` |

Or run all the checks at once from the lab folder:

```bash
./verify.sh
```

```
Checking lab first-lab
  PASS  n1 is running
  PASS  n1 eth1 has 10.0.12.1/30
  PASS  n2 is running
  PASS  n2 eth1 has 10.0.12.2/30
  PASS  n1 pings n2 (10.0.12.1 -> 10.0.12.2), 0% loss

All checks passed.
```

Any `FAIL` line says which check failed. If every check passes, Containerlab is installed and working.

### Remove the lab

```bash
containerlab destroy -t first-lab.clab.yml
```

`destroy` removes the containers and the link. The folder `clab-first-lab/` next to the topology file holds the lab's
generated files and is left in place; it is recreated on the next deploy.

## Upgrade, pin a version or uninstall

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Upgrade to the latest release | `sudo -E containerlab version upgrade`, or `sudo apt update && sudo apt install containerlab` |
| List the versions available | `apt-cache madison containerlab` |
| Install a specific version | `sudo apt install containerlab=0.82.0` (if a newer version is installed, apt asks you to confirm the downgrade) |
| Stop it upgrading (and allow again) | `sudo apt-mark hold containerlab` (`sudo apt-mark unhold containerlab`) |
| Uninstall | `sudo apt remove containerlab` |

Everyone in a workshop should run the same Containerlab version, so install the same version on every host and hold it.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| `permission denied ... /var/run/docker.sock` | Your user is not in the `docker` group yet. Run `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, then log out and in (or reboot) |
| `containerlab deploy` asks for root or refuses to run | Your user is not in `clab_admins` yet. Run `sudo usermod -aG clab_admins $USER`, then log out and in |
| `id -nG` still shows the old groups | Reboot. A background user session kept the old list |
| `apt` cannot find `containerlab` | Check `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/netdevops.list` exists, then run `sudo apt update` |
| Deploy fails with errors that mention IPv6 | IPv6 is disabled in the kernel (for example `ipv6.disable=1` on the kernel command line). Re-enable it; Containerlab expects it |
| Image pull fails | Check the host's internet access and DNS. Behind a proxy, configure Docker's proxy settings |
